extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of literature familiar with Renaissance essays; readers of Montaigne / classic philosophical prose
extracted.subtask_description: Interpreting and drawing practical/writing guidelines from Michel de Montaigne's Essays (Cotton translation), including his remarks on truth, self-writing, conscience, pleasure, and style. Useful for readers, essayists, and literary students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plainness and simplicity as a desirable condition
rubrics_metrics.description: The least contemptible condition of men is that of plainness and simplicity, seated in the lowest degree, inviting a more regular course.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value plain, simple manners; such simplicity often aligns better with true philosophy than affected refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Country manners better suited to true philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: The rude manners and language of country people are commonly better suited to the rule and prescription of true philosophy than those of philosophers themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer natural, unadorned behavior and speech as more congruent with philosophical truth than polished affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Autobiographical writing should be warranted by worthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: It misbecomes ordinary men to give their own character; writing oneself is more excusable in rare and famous men whose life and opinions may serve for example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only those with qualities worthy of imitation have a strong claim to publish autobiographical accounts; others should be modest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write for friends/private use, avoid public ostentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The essays are addressed to a private circle ('you and I are talking in private'), not meant as public pomp or to swell pages with empty trifles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a intimate tone; avoid writing intended primarily to display or aggrandize the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-writing as self-cultivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne claims that making a continual and exact account of himself has tempered and composed him; the book has made him as much as he made the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use personal writing to discipline thought, reflect, and form one’s character; recording small thoughts trains the mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use writing to vent where civility forbids public reproach
rubrics_metrics.description: When civility and reason prevent open reproof, the writer may 'disgorge' himself in writing, sometimes with public instruction in view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writing can serve as a safe vehicle for criticism, satire, or corrective remarks that cannot be delivered face-to-face.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth is the foundational virtue; lying dissolves social ties
rubrics_metrics.description: To be true is the beginning of a great virtue; falsifying words betrays public society because language is the interpreter of the soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize truth in speech and writing; lying undermines trust and the bonds of government and society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproach for lying signals self-defence and perceived cowardice
rubrics_metrics.description: People are most offended by accusations of lying; resenting that reproach often serves as a way to defend a fault, and eating one’s words implies cowardice before men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that reactions to being called a liar may be more about self-image than moral repair; accusations of lying carry particular social stigma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissimulation is a notable quality of the age
rubrics_metrics.description: Dissimulation (hypocrisy, concealment) has become a marked trait of contemporary manners; people fashion themselves to it as an exercise of honour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat claims of sincere appearances skeptically; be alert to the prevalence and social function of dissimulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: The laws and practices of giving the lie are culturally variable
rubrics_metrics.description: The customs and laws about 'giving the lie' and honour vary across times and peoples; among Romans and Greeks invective could be practiced without escalating to violence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that verbal norms of honour differ historically and culturally; don't assume modern practices are universal or ancient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty of conscience is politically double-edged
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowing liberty of conscience can either scatter and sow division (inflaming civil dissension) or mollify and appease a people (dulling the edge of novelty and difficulty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that toleration may be used as a tool either to divide opponents or to pacify a populace; assess motives and consequences in political uses of tolerance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zealotry harms learning (book-burning and censorship)
rubrics_metrics.description: Religious zeal in early times caused great losses by destroying pagan books; excessive zeal led to the abolition and censorship of writings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protect intellectual heritage from ideologically-motivated destruction; recognize the long-term cultural damage of censorious zeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: No pleasure or good is entirely pure; everything mixes with some ill
rubrics_metrics.description: The elements we enjoy are always changed for our use; our extremest pleasure contains some groaning and complaint—pleasure is never unalloyed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating pleasures or goods, account for their attendant pains or costs; avoid the myth of pure, unmitigated delight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Even the best virtue contains some tincture of vice
rubrics_metrics.description: On introspection, even the best virtues possess some human mixture; Plato's pure virtue would reveal faint jarring notes upon close self-listening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be modest about claims of moral purity; accept complexity and partial impurity in moral character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law and justice necessarily contain some injustice for the public good
rubrics_metrics.description: Great public examples and laws have mixtures of iniquity, which public utility may recompense for wrongs done to particular men (Tacitus cited).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In public policy and law, accept trade-offs between individual injustices and perceived public utility; be alert to the moral cost of collective decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessive subtilty and speculative exactness impede practical action
rubrics_metrics.description: Penetrating light and subtlety can be too much for business; one must blunt or veil thought somewhat to fit dark, earthly life—practical affairs often suit less speculative souls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer simpler, pragmatic instruments for action; avoid over-analysis that prevents decision and execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endeavouring to be brief can produce obscurity
rubrics_metrics.description: A stated maxim: 'Endeavouring to be brief, I become obscure.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance brevity with clarity; excessive compression of thought can render writing unintelligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speech and action animate words more than writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Motion and action animate the word; speaking can be more lively than writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging rhetoric or persuasion, privilege spoken delivery/context for its animating effect; written form may need compensatory devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: A generous heart should not belie its own thoughts (honesty in benevolence)
rubrics_metrics.description: An axiom in the bookmarks: 'A generous heart ought not to belie its own thoughts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generosity should be sincere; benevolent dispositions demand truthfulness between feeling and expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: The reward of well-done work is the doing itself
rubrics_metrics.description: Another aphorism: 'The reward of a thing well done is to have done it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value intrinsic satisfaction from workmanship or moral action rather than external rewards or reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of personal memorabilia and small tokens to preserve memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne preserves writings, seals, a sword and his father's staves as treasured relics; such objects transmit the manners and fortunes of ancestors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material artifacts and family objects help maintain familial memory and continuity; consider preserving small tokens as mnemonic devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording trivial thoughts cultivates meditative habit
rubrics_metrics.description: Recording 'little thoughts' and whims trains the fancy to meditate in some method rather than rove at random.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep a habit of noting small thoughts to build reflective discipline and avoid aimless mental roaming—practical advice for essayists and journalers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry demands seriousness (limit folly in poetic art)
rubrics_metrics.description: From the bookmarks: 'A man may play the fool in everything else, but not in poetry' and 'Nothing is more confident than a bad poet.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat poetic art with seriousness and craft; avoid frivolity in poetry and be wary of overconfidence without skill.
